title: Of the Longed-for Victory...
text:
Of the longed-for victory

lost now, all hope gone,

only death may be able

to ease our misfortune.

Before the Christians' fire

resistance is futile,

and all yields before the edge

of their cutting swords.

Beneath their formidable blows

perhaps has fallen

the bravest cacique

of the land of Agueinaba;

without his mighty breath

and without his arm, oh grief!

what shall we attempt

in so bitter a plight?

Christians never die,

Borinquen keeps its empire;

ah, let us hide our lives

in the rugged mountains.


Thus the Indian hosts

cried out in their grief

when, one day at Yagüeca,

they saw their pride destroyed.

Then, united with the chieftain

who was once their hope,

the intrepid Humacao,

who gave his name to the region,

they carried their sorrow

to the high sierra

that greets the sun at its rising

and guards the Caribbean Sea.

There, on that eminence,

the cacique resisted

the might of the brave Christian champion

for a long age,

now storming the plains,

now making of his gorges

a dreadful bulwark,

witness to a hundred deeds.

There fell, the last of them,

of the Borinquen hosts—.

And they say that his shadow

on those rugged summits

from time to time appears

to neighboring eyes.


I imagine that his spirit

was bathed in holy light,

with which heaven, in its mercy,

shines there upon souls:

that when he fell for his law,

faithful to it though pagan,

eternal mercy

took his ignorance into account.

And ever since, wandering,

when he sees the worthy

redeeming cross raised in his land,

he kneels and lifts a tender prayer

from the height

that was his glorious castle,

so that his beloved land

may owe its well-being to the cross—.

Such are the mournful echoes

that, on a solitary night,

are heard in the heights

of the rugged mountain.

Such the wandering shadow

seen kneeling

on the gigantic Yunque

when the moon bathes it—.

When the Christian flock saw

the cacique's pride,

the tireless courage

with which he fought for his homeland,

and that his endeavor was madness,

it gave the region the name

of Sierra del Loquillo,

and now it is called Luquillo.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem's historical-legendary voice, Borinquen and Taíno place names, and its recurring mountain-shadow imagery. The source has stray terminal hyphens in several lines; these are retained as em dashes to preserve the punctuation's visible ambiguity.

title: On Looking at My Cheeks, Red Only Yesterday...
text:
On looking at my cheeks, red only yesterday,

I have felt autumn; its old age's ailments

have filled me with fear; the mirror has told me

that it snows in my hair while the leaves fall…


What a curious fate! It has knocked at my doors

in the full springtime to offer me snow,

and my hands grow icy beneath the light pressure

of a hundred blue roses dead upon their fingers.


I already feel myself wholly invaded by ice;

my teeth chatter while the sun outside

sets patches of gold, as in spring,

and laughs in the sky's unfathomable depth.


And I weep slowly, with a cursed pain…

with a pain that weighs upon all my fibers,

O pale death that offers me a wedding

and the blurred mystery laden with infinity!


But I rebel!… How can this human form,

which cost matter so many transformations,

kill, inside my breast, all my illusions

and bring me night at almost full morning?
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet-like quatrain structure and the poem's reversal of spring into premature winter. The source reads “enson[d]ada” (apparently a typo for “insondada,” unfathomable); the English uses “unfathomable” while noting the source irregularity here.

title: This Afternoon
text:
Now I want to love something far away…
some divine man
who is like a bird in his sweetness,
who has known countless women
and knows other lands, and whose word
blooms on his lips, perfumed:
like a virgin forest beneath the wind…


And I want to love him now. The afternoon is
soft and tranquil like thick moss,
my mouth trembles, and my fine fingers
slowly undo my braids.


I feel a vague murmur… All the earth
is singing sweetly… Far away,
the forests have filled with corollas,
the streams overflow their beds
and the waters seep into the earth
as my eyes seep into the eyes
I dream of, enraptured…


But…
the sun is already sinking behind the mountains,
the birds huddle in their nests,
the afternoon must die and he is far away…
far away like this sun that forever
departs and leaves me, with my hands
buried in my braids, my mouth
moist and trembling, my soul
made subtle, afire with hope
of this infinite love that makes me
sweet and beautiful…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the speaker's sensuous, dreamlike progression from the late afternoon landscape to the absent beloved and keeps the short “But…” turn as a hinge.

title: Things That Die Never Rise Again...
text:
Things that die never rise again,

things that die never return again.

The vessels break and the glass that remains

is dust forever and forever will be!


When the buds fall from the branch

they will never bloom a second time…

The flowers broken by the impious wind

are spent forever, forevermore!


The days that were, the lost days,

the inert days will not return!

How sad the hours that slipped away

beneath solitude's beating wing!


How sad the shadows, the baleful shadows,

the shadows made by our wickedness!

O things gone, things withered,

the celestial things that leave us so!


Heart… be still!… Cover yourself with sores!…

—with infected sores—cover yourself with evil!…

Let everyone who comes die upon touching you,

cursed heart that vexes my longing!


Farewell forever, all my sweetnesses!

Farewell, my joy full of goodness!

O dead things, withered things,

the celestial things that never return!…
editorial_note: The translation retains the insistent repetitions, exclamations, and direct address that make the poem a chant of irreversible loss.

title: The Dream
text:
I saw two red suns ruling the sky
Topaz lights beaded on their rays
and I stretched out both my hands, hungry for infinity,
to clasp within them an ineffable myth.


The two red pupils, like roses of the sky,
blinded my pupils, proud in their longing
to gaze directly at the diamond glints.


Then, like the crack of knots breaking…
Proud storms threading themselves through the seas;
birth of the gods… A god's groan…
and mouths biting one another in a supreme farewell!


Later, a sonata sweeter than honey;
the agony of lilies in that garden.
a palace of gold and gold where a sorceress dwells
who has slept a hundred years beneath an evil curse.


And then white hands scattering roses
over the hidden, serene soul of things…
And a silence of death, weary and sepulchral,
where the poisonous lotus of evil takes hold.


And then morning arriving at the windows
of the wretched room where I bite my sorrows…
And then another day sketched in the weeping
of my sunless days, of my goldless suns!…
editorial_note: The translation keeps the dream's abrupt cinematic sequence—red suns, divine rupture, enchanted palace, deathly silence, and the return to the poor room—along with its surreal repetitions.

title: Seeking Roots for Wings...
text:
Seeking roots for wings

his forehead

shifts

to the right

and left.


And over the whirlpool

of his face

it fixes itself,

a curtain of the beyond,

curved and broad.


A creature

screams in his nose,

which tries to crush it,

enraged…


A Greek bursts forth

through his distant eyes.


A Greek

whom the Andalusian hills

of his cheekbones

and the trembling valley

of his mouth

smother in vines.


His throat leaps

outward

begging

for the moon-shaped razor

of sharp waters.


Cut it off.

From north to south.

From east to west.


Let the head fly,

the head alone,

wounded by black

sea waves…


And by satyr conches

that fall upon it

like bellflowers

on the face

of an ancient mask.


Silence

his wooden voice,

hollow,

wrapped up

in the nasal catacombs.


Free him from it,

and from its sweet arms,

and from its earthen body.


Only force on him,

before hurling him

into space,

the arch of his eyebrows

until you make them bridges

over the Atlantic,

over the Pacific…


Across which his eyes,

lost ships,

may travel

without ports

or shores…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem's fractured visual syntax, person shifts, anatomical surrealism, and abrupt imperatives. “Cortádsela” is rendered as the direct command “Cut it off,” without resolving the source's unusual object reference.

title: The Kind Invitation
text:
Come closer, poet; my soul is sober,
it knows nothing of love—of earthly love—
its love is loftier and better.


I will not ask for kisses from your lips.
I will not drink from your crystal glass,
the glass is fragile and loves the immortal.


Come closer, poet without suspicion…
offer me the grace of your hands,
there will be no idle thoughts in my fancy.


Would you go to the woods with a book,
a gentle book full of beauty?…
We could read some pleasant passage.


I will place in my voice the religion of your soul,
the religion of pity and harmony
that in everything is kin to my own grief.


I will ask you to tell me of your loves
and some story which, because it is old,
will give us the perfume of an old rose.


I will say nothing of myself
because I have no perfumed flowers
that could thus be made into a story.


The chest—an urn for my bygone dreams—
shall not be opened, ending their slumber,
to show you their bitter contents.


I will do everything seeking your joy
and I will be as kind to you
as the perfume of the old rose.


The invitation stands… sincere and noble.
Do you wish to be my good poet-friend
and share only your sorrow with me?
editorial_note: The stored source has OCR errors in the closing stanza and “El cofre y una urna.” The translation follows Alfonsina Storni’s 1916 first edition, La inquietud del rosal, p. 42 (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bc/La_inquietud_del_rosal_%281916%29.pdf): “El cofre y urna,” “La invitación está,” and the opening question mark before “¿Quieres.”

title: Prayer to Betrayal
text:
Love… love! You betray my desires,
my sadness, my effort. When I sank
the illusion into death's shadow,
you revive its corpse, you master it,


and deliver me bound
like a defeated martyr…
Love… love! Your wings have beaten
at the soul's doors, softly…
Your cooing lied to me, I do not ignore it,


but I was cowardly, and with wings
foreboding and tragic you have made me
—a mantle all white and all rose!
Betrayal! Betrayal! Your fine dagger thrust


bleeds my vein and is bound to bring me death,
and I cannot, nor do I wish to, curse you.
You have returned, love, you have returned!
like a child suddenly startled,


my soul takes pains to receive you
and fear; perhaps it trembles for its flowers,
which opened only just when your wings,
fine love, called me, called me.


Enter, traitor! Attempt some miracle!
Let your living breath pass like a
flame of life where the soul may
awaken to sweet Spring


and forget the merciless winter!
Enter, traditore! And overcome me, stifle me;
make me forget the storm gone by,
lull me, put me to sleep, and see to it


that I die in the dream of your deceit,
while you softly sing to me the joy
of the sun's Eastertide!
editorial_note: The stored source contains OCR errors. The translation follows Alfonsina Storni’s 1916 first edition, La inquietud del rosal, pp. 22–23 (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bc/La_inquietud_del_rosal_%281916%29.pdf): “Revives,” “agoreras,” “fina,” and singular “tiembla.” The Italian “traditore” is retained from the edition.

title: The Sick Swan
text:
There is a swan dying, enclosed by a palace.
A mysterious swan in a robe of silk
that, instead of gliding on the gentle current,
comes to a standstill, weary of staring into space.


The swan is an invalid who adores the golden God;
the sun, father of races, makes its agony fertile,
therefore its sadness is a symphony
of flowers half-opening in the shadows of weeping.


Its breast is crossed by a mad dagger,
drop by drop its blood dissolves into the lake
and the blue waters are enchanted beneath the magician's
power—the rubies its evil distills.


This swan's soul is a sensitive plant;
do not raise your voice beside the pond
if you do not want the swan, with its beak, to tear out
the dagger that sustains its furtive existence.


Old legends tell that love is ill.
That its enormous heart has been multiplied a hundredfold
and that within it, like the Crucified,
it bears a pain that shelters every human pain.


And the legends tell that it is a poet-swan…
That the magic of rhythm has anointed its throat
and it sings for no reason, as the stream sings
the crystalline rhyme of its restless current.


One night I dreamed that in the old palace
I was the swan, weary of staring into space.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the swan’s decadent symbolism, the personified “golden God,” and the final dream-frame. The source’s “tristezza” is rendered as “sadness,” and the missing space in “vozal lado” is restored.

title: Go on, Take Flight, Make Yourself a Bee...
text:
Go on, take flight, make yourself a bee,

In the garden poppies are in bloom,

and the fine nectar fills their cups;

tomorrow your soul will be old.


Go on, let yourself fly, make yourself a dove,

travel the woods and peck at grains,

eat crumbs from different hands,

and bite the flesh of fragrant apples.


Go on, take flight, be a swallow,

seek the beach of golden suns,

taste spring and its treasure,

spring is unique and divine.


You are dying of thirst: I must not oppress you so…

Go on, walk through the world, learn;

your ship is waiting on the sea:

set out rowing toward the finest enchantment.


Run, walk farther, that is too little…

There are still things your hand longs for,

run, walk, turn, climb, and fly:

taste everything because everything is beautiful.


Fly away… my love does not hold you back,

How I understand you, Beloved, how I understand you!

Let my life weep… let my heart grieve…

Take flight, Love, I understand you.


The soul silent… the heart broken,

I release your wings… go… but I await you.

How will you bring your heart back, traveler?

I will pity a defeated heart.


So that you may cure such thirst by drinking,

there are many paths for you…

But night is falling; do not hurry…

They all lead to me…
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's repeated release commands, its sequence of bee, dove, and swallow images, and the final reversal in which every road leads back to the speaker.

title: Caprice 2
text:
Search my eyes, surprise my mouth,
hold this mad head between your hands;
give me poison to drink, the wicked poison
that wets the lips despite being good.


But do not ask me, do not ask me anything
of why I cried so much last night;
we women cry without knowing, simply because.
Such tears are a trivial matter.


It is plain we carry inside a hidden sea,
a sea somewhat awkward, slightly hidden,
that peeks into our eyes quite often
and we even manage it with pliant skill.


Do not ask, beloved, you must suspect it:
last night the sea was not still.
Nothing more. Storms come and go
on a wind that marks a new coast for us each time.


Yes, vain butterflies over a January garden,
our inner life is all without balance and hollow.
A crystal gleam, a carnival fruit
decorated in the scales of evil's serpents.


That is how we are, is it not? The poet said it:
we desire and relish the honey in every cup
and have a little tow in our brains.


Very well. No, do not ask me. A woman's clumsiness,
a caprice, my beloved, it must be caprice.
Oh, let me laugh. Don't you see what a beautiful afternoon?
Prick your hands and cut me a rose.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the intimate, self-mocking voice and the poem’s sea-as-feeling metaphor; the dismissive “pasaje baladí” is rendered as “a trivial matter.”

title: Swallows
text:
They are the sweet messengers of sadness…
they are little black birds, black as night.
Black as pain!


The sweet swallows that leave in winter
and abandon the nest, empty and alone,
to cross the sea!


Each time I see one I feel a subtle chill…
Oh! Little black birds, restless little birds,
lovers of April!


Oh! Poor swallows that go to seek,
like emigrants, in foreign lands,
the morsel of bread!


Swallows, come near! Swallows, come!
Come in springtime, with mourning wings,
come near to me!


Hold me on your wings… Hold me and cross
with a single flight, the eternal, ever more eternal
immensity of the sea…


Do you know how one travels to the land of the sun?…
Do you know where eternal spring is found,
the fountain of love?…


Carry me, swallows! Carry me! Do not fear!
I am a bohemian, a poor bohemian—
carry me where you are going!


Do you not know, wandering swallows, do you not know
that my soul is ill because I cannot leave,
flying, too?


Swallows, come near! Swallows, come!
Come in springtime, with mourning wings,
come near to me!


Come! Carry me quickly to try my fortune!…
What a pity, little ones, that you do not have wings
woven in blue!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the songlike refrains, the swallows’ “mourning wings,” and the speaker’s immigrant and bohemian longing. The singular “la veo” is rendered naturally as “I see one.”

title: You Want Me White
text:
You want me white,

you want me made of foam,

you want me of mother-of-pearl.

That I be a lily,

chaste above all others,

of faint perfume.

A closed corolla.


Not a ray of moonlight

may have filtered through me.

May no daisy

call itself my sister.

You want me snowy,

you want me white,

you want me dawn-white.


You who had every

cup within reach,

your lips purple

with fruits and honey.

You who at the banquet

covered in vine leaves

left your flesh

celebrating Bacchus.

You who in the gardens

black with Deceit,

dressed in red,

ran toward Ruin.


You who still keep

your skeleton intact

by miracles

I cannot fathom,

you demand me white

(God forgive you),

you demand me chaste

(God forgive you),

you demand me dawn-white!


Flee toward the woods,

go to the mountain;

cleanse your mouth;

live in huts;

touch with your hands

the wet earth;

feed your body

on bitter root;

drink from the rocks;

sleep upon frost;

renew your tissues

with saltpeter and water:


Speak with the birds

and rise at dawn.

And when your flesh

has been returned to you,

and when you have placed

within it the soul

that in the bedrooms

was left tangled,

then, good man,

demand me white,

demand me snowy,

demand me chaste.
editorial_note: The translation retains the poem’s accusatory repetition, Bacchic imagery, and imperative cleansing sequence. The irregular “lévate al alba” is rendered as “rise at dawn.”

title: Sweet and Somber
text:
Where are you now? You were so sweet, child,

with blond hair and eyes of steel…

Child who, despite myself, was my prisoner,

O my pale child!


So humble was the kiss that kissed my feet,

with such deep delight, with such limpid complaint,

that as time passes and moves away

my feet desire it.


You would fall silent on golden afternoons

when a book in our hands brought us sadness,

and then your head would fall upon my knees

like a flake of gold.


Then perfumes rose from your soul

to the tired soul that weighed upon my breast…

O your soul… as fresh as a fern branch!

It rose in perfumes.


Child whom I adored… O your white tears

that watered the impossible word in abundance,

I was your discreet sister, sad and sensitive child,

of white tears.


I loved no one as I loved you, sweet and somber child

who wept in my arms over my prudent turning away.

My memory will love you without end,

sweet and somber child.


Let us go toward the trees… Sleep

will come upon us by celestial grace.

Let us go toward the trees; the night

will be soft for us, sadness light.


Let us go toward the trees, the soul

drowsed by wild perfume,

but be quiet, do not speak, be merciful;

do not wake the sleeping birds.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem's intimate address, the repeated end-words of its quatrains, and the final movement into a hushed forest.

title: Rise Again
text:
I passed through the sieve of every sorrow

And I am purified. I cry out for a new life!

A life that will be like a rhythm of silk!

Sweetness and more sweetness! The stillness of an afternoon.


Delightful and sunlit, the little house with ivy

and a patch of sky where the soul tangles itself.


No longing except a child's longing,

to have the swallows of an eternal stillness

and to feel myself so good… so deeply good!…


To read nothing, nothing, except in the lavish,

infinite and precious book of nature

and sip its truths with hope wide open!…


To rise into a new life. To work the miracle

of covering the wound in my veins with jasmine

and making a white song from the remains of tragedy.


To have a heart made of a flash of light,

to have a heart made into a nest of gems

so that other new corollas may always open.


To cross through life with wings in the soul,

with wings in the body, with wings in thought

and a slight fondness for approaching death.


To forgive, forgive, to bear no grudge;

to give everything to oblivion and weep in the quiet

solitude of night with pearly tears.


Pearls of annunciation, of oblivion, of joy,

of sweetness, and the delight of feeling serene

and understanding life as a rhythm of silk.


Today I desire it so… today, a feast day,

and I have much of Christmas Eve within my soul…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the prayerlike infinitives, the recurring silk-rhythm image, and the movement from purification through forgiveness toward renewal. The source contains compressed punctuation in “Purificada.¡Clamo” and “¡tan”; the English restores spacing while retaining the exclamatory force.
